clues.title: Plate: long white, blue strip each side
text: Modern French plates are long and white, with **blue strips on both sides** of the plate. The left strip will be more visible than the right strip.
Some older French plates lack the right blue strip, with the rear plate being **yellow**. These are very rare in newer coverage.
NOTE: Italian plates also have two blue strips, which are equally visible. In addition, Italian front plates are considerably shorter.
clues.summary: Long white plates with a blue strip on both sides, the left more visible. Old rear plates can be yellow and lack the right strip, but are rare. Italy has two equal blue strips and shorter front plates.

differs.how: two equally visible blue strips, shorter front plate

clues.title: Language: accents é à è â ê î ô ç and œ
text: **French** is a Romance language that is closely related to languages like Catalan, Spanish and Italian. It uses these diacritics and special letters:
- Accent aigu: é
- Accent grave: à, è, ù
- Accent circonflexe: â, ê, î, ô, û
- Trema: ë, ï, ü, ÿ
- Ligature: œ
- [Cédille](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cedilla): ç with a small hook
In addition, the -ux suffix is only found in French.
NOTE: Other European countries with sizable francophone populations include Belgium, Luxembourg, Monaco and Switzerland.
clues.summary: A Romance language with accents (é, è, à, â, ê, î, ô, û), tréma (ë, ï, ü), ç and œ. Words ending in -ux are only French. Belgium, Luxembourg, Monaco and Switzerland also speak it.

clues.title: Language: street is 'rue'
text: The French word for street is “**rue**”.
clues.summary: The word for street is 'rue'. Belgium uses it on street signs too.

clues.title: Bollard: round white, pointed top, reflector band
text: The French bollard is extremely recognizable and appears very often. It is a **round white post with a pointed top** and a reflector band going all the way around. The band can be grey or red. Some rare variations have a [fully red top](https://maps.app.goo.gl/1zSoGbpiKic3nAxM6).
NOTE: A bollard that is commonly found in [Scotland](https://goo.gl/maps/CyjNmHyh5zyKv7qR7) looks similar, but has a blunt top instead of a pointed one.
clues.summary: A round white post with a pointed top and a reflector band all the way around, grey or red. Rare ones have a fully red top. Scottish bollards look similar but have a blunt top.

differs.how: Scottish version has a blunt top, not pointed

clues.title: Bollard: round white with two indented bands
text: A different round white bollard, with two reflective indented bands, is unique to France.
You can also find this design in other colours like [green](https://goo.gl/maps/HiePkuYXrAFBQbyu9) or [yellow](https://goo.gl/maps/uKExi7xcUZjGZt316).
clues.summary: A round white post with two reflective indented bands. Also in green or yellow versions. Only found here.

clues.title: Bollard: wedge shape, wide white reflectors
text: Less common wedge**-**shaped bollards with **wide** **rectangular white reflectors** on both the front and back are also unique to France.
clues.summary: A wedge-shaped bollard with wide rectangular white reflectors on front and back. Less common, and only found here.

clues.title: Pole: concrete with step-like indents
text: Concrete poles with step-like indents are common in France. They are referred to as **ladder** or **waffle poles** by the community.
NOTE: They are also common in Spain.
clues.summary: Concrete poles with step-like indents, called ladder or waffle poles. Common in Spain too.

clues.title: Pole: wood or thin octagonal metal
text: Wooden poles and thin [octagonal metal poles](https://goo.gl/maps/HQZMGmGXLKRX2s7y6) are very common in rural areas and small towns.
clues.summary: Wooden poles and thin octagonal metal poles are very common in the countryside and small towns.

clues.title: Pole: small blue plate
text: Small** blue **rectangular markings on** utility poles** are unique to France. They are often referred to as ‘stickers’ by the community, but are actually small plates.
You will find these plates on almost all wooden and metallic poles, but not as often on ladder poles.
clues.summary: Small blue rectangular plates on utility poles, found only here. On almost all wooden and metal poles, less often on ladder poles.

clues.title: Pole: diamond top with three wires
text: Diamond shaped pole tops with three wires are commonly called “French poletops” within the community. They are most frequently found on top of ladder poles.
NOTE: Within Europe, “French poletops” in conjunction with ladder poles are also common in Spain.
clues.summary: A diamond-shaped pole top with three wires, mostly on top of ladder poles. Spain has this combination too.

clues.title: Pole: arrowhead top, insulators on top
text: Some variations of the French pole tops have the insulators on top. These variations may resemble an arrowhead and are unique to France.
clues.summary: Some pole tops have the insulators on top and look like an arrowhead. Only found here.

clues.title: Google car: low-mounted camera, big round blur
text: France has Generation 4 “smallcam” coverage, which is mounted lower than regular Generation 4 and has a relatively big circular blur with a small protrusion at the front. The blur can also be fully transparent, making it harder to spot.
NOTE: Most of Western Europe also has smallcam.
clues.summary: A Gen 4 camera mounted lower than normal, with a fairly big round blur and a small bump at the front. The blur can be see-through. Most of Western Europe has it.

clues.title: Sign: small yellow road number plate, D-road
text: Small **yellow signs** displaying the road number, which typically starts with a “**D**”, are unique to France. They are commonly placed on top of directional signs or town entry signs.
clues.summary: Small yellow signs with the road number, usually starting with D, often on top of direction or town entry signs. Only found here.

clues.title: Sign: white direction sign, offset black outline
text: French directional signs are usually white with a black outline slightly offset from the edge. They have an arrow-like shape, with the black border getting thicker at the point.
Highway directions have either a [blue or green background](https://goo.gl/maps/8jKUAjSqdf9AJcLM9).
Smaller places and points of interest are frequently written in an italic font.
clues.summary: White direction signs with a black outline slightly in from the edge, arrow-shaped with a thicker border at the point. Highways are blue or green. Small places are often in italics.

clues.title: Sign: town entry with red border, thin white outline
text: Town entrance signs in France have a red border with a thin white outline.
clues.summary: Town entry signs have a red border with a thin white outline.

clues.title: Sign: red border with thin white outline
text: French road signs have a red border with a thin white outline. You will often find white rectangular signs with black text below traffic signs.
NOTE: Road signs in Spain have a [thick red border](https://maps.app.goo.gl/49ec9Xf89vko3Tbr5) that goes all the way to the edge.
clues.summary: Road signs have a red border with a thin white outline, and often a white rectangular sign with black text below. Spain's red border is thick and goes to the edge.

differs.how: thick red border going all the way to the edge

clues.title: Sign: flat rectangular signposts
text: Many traffic signs in France have flat rectangular signposts.
_Signposts, along with signbacks, can be dyed with unorthodox colours, more so than in other countries. Some of those are regional, which you can learn more about in the regionguessing section._
NOTE: The only other European countries with flat signposts are Portugal, Spain, and Andorra.
clues.summary: Many traffic signs sit on flat rectangular posts, and posts or backs may be oddly coloured. Only Portugal, Spain and Andorra also use flat posts in Europe.

clues.title: Sign: very short signposts
text: Traffic signs with particularly **short signposts** are very common in France.
clues.summary: Traffic signs on particularly short posts are very common.

clues.title: Chevron: white arrows on blue, one to five
text: France uses chevrons with white arrows on a blue background. They can have a wide amount of arrows, ranging from one to five.
NOTE: The only other European country with this colour scheme is Spain, where you will only find chevrons with two or four arrows.
clues.summary: Chevrons with white arrows on blue, with one to five arrows. Spain has this colour scheme too, but only with two or four arrows.

differs.how: only two or four arrows

clues.title: Sign: pedestrian sign with 5 stripes, split head
text: Pedestrian crossing signs in France have five stripes and a disconnected head on the person. They have the usual white border of French traffic signs.
Less commonly, you can find a design with [two dashed lines](https://goo.gl/maps/iD7GdGUA7Ew3h8oa7) instead of stripes.
clues.summary: Pedestrian crossing sign with five stripes and a head detached from the body, with the usual wide white border. Less commonly two dashed lines instead of stripes.

clues.title: Route marker: yellow or red semicircle on white
text: Kilometre markers in France most commonly have a yellow or red semicircle on top of a white rectangle. They can be found in the form of a waystone or as a flat sign and can be either [parallel](https://goo.gl/maps/8KpoMhXGetkA7qeR9) or [perpendicular](https://goo.gl/maps/WJHfU8tnG9qfZoyDA) to the road. Major highways can have [square markers](https://maps.app.goo.gl/RTdHYF79SdUZFLTt7) with a red top.
clues.summary: Km markers usually have a yellow or red semicircle on top of a white rectangle, as a waystone or flat sign, parallel or perpendicular to the road. Big highways have square markers with a red top.

clues.title: Road lines: long spaced-out edge dashes
text: Typical French roads have long spaced out dashes on the outside.
clues.summary: Typical roads have long dashes with big gaps on the outside edge.

clues.title: Road lines: centre dashes of two offset blocks
text: These middle road lines, where each dash consists of two **offset blocks**, are unique to France. They are not extremely common, but when you see them, you can safely guess France.
clues.summary: Centre lines where each dash is two offset blocks. Not very common, but a sure sign of the country.

clues.title: Road lines: unusually long centre dashes
text: Middle lines with **dashes that are longer than usual** can be a good clue for France.
NOTE: Unusually long dashes are also common in the UK.
clues.summary: Unusually long centre dashes are a good clue. The UK has long dashes too.

differs.how: also has very long centre dashes

clues.title: Road lines: end-of-passing-zone arrows
text: These arrows on the road signalling the end of a passing zone are only found in a couple of European countries, including France. In France, the middle dashes will be very close together in these areas.

NOTE: Other countries where this style of arrow can be found are Spain, Portugal and Romania. These arrows can also be found in the UK, but they will point towards the left lane instead of the right one.
clues.summary: Arrows on the road at the end of a passing zone, with the centre dashes very close together. Spain, Portugal and Romania have them too. In the UK they point to the left lane.

differs.how: arrows point to the left lane

clues.title: Guardrail: A-type, usually no reflectors
text: France uses A-type guardrails, usually without reflectors. On rare occasions, you can find [thin B-type](https://maps.app.goo.gl/LZPs77QN14xKdL3RA), the standard guardrail in Czechia and Slovakia.
NOTE: Spanish, Andorran and Belgian guardrails use yellow reflectors.
clues.summary: Mostly A-type guardrails without reflectors. Thin B-type, the standard in Czechia and Slovakia, appears rarely. Spanish, Andorran and Belgian guardrails have yellow reflectors.

differs.how: yellow reflectors on guardrails
yellow reflectors on guardrails

clues.title: Sign: red-white-red tall rectangles on sticks
text: Roads may be lined by tall rectangles on a stick in the colours of the Austrian flag, which are not found elsewhere.
clues.summary: Roadsides may have tall rectangles on sticks in the colours of the Austrian flag, found nowhere else.

clues.title: Houses: stone, pastel, gable roofs, orange tiles
text: French architecture largely consists of stone houses, which will normally be either unpainted or painted in greyish or yellow pastel colours. The roofs will typically have a simple [gable](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gable_roof) design, with orange tiles or less commonly black slates. Townhouses will often lay wall to wall along the road.

Do note that France has some of the most diverse regional architecture of any European country, so don’t be surprised to see towns that look significantly different from the previously described architecture.
clues.summary: Mostly stone houses, unpainted or in grey or yellow pastels, with simple gable roofs of orange tiles or sometimes black slate. Townhouses often touch along the road. Regional styles vary a lot.

clues.title: House number: blue serif plates
text: House numbers in France are most commonly blue, typically written in a serif font with slightly exaggerated shapes. This is most useful when differentiating from Italy, which almost never uses blue house number signs.
NOTE: Similar designs can be found in all other neighbouring, as well as many other, countries.
clues.summary: House numbers are most often blue in a serif font with slightly exaggerated shapes. Italy almost never uses blue house numbers.

differs.how: almost never uses blue house numbers

clues.title: Cars: Peugeot, Renault, Citroën
text: French car brands Peugeot, Renault and Citroën together make up almost half of all cars in France.
NOTE: These car brands are also common in linguistically related neighbouring countries.
clues.summary: Peugeot, Renault and Citroën make up almost half of all cars. Neighbouring French-speaking countries have them too.

clues.title: Regions: 13 regions and 96 departments
text: This guide will mainly operate with two types of administrative divisions: [**regions**](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regions_of_France), totalling at **13** in European France, and **96 **[**departments**](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Departments_of_France), which appear on Google Maps as the primary administrative divisions. Other rarer divisions you may come across include [pre-2016 regions](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/d/df/Map_Carte_des_Anciennes_R%C3%A9gions_2015.png) and [historical provinces](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/d/d9/France_in_1789.svg).
Departments are often named after physical geographical features and their logos may show up on various infrastructure, shown in the next tip.
_You can practise them with [this quiz](https://geo.emily.bz/map-quiz/france/departments)._
clues.summary: The guide uses 13 regions and 96 departments. Departments are named after geographic features and their logos appear on infrastructure.

clues.title: Phone numbers: 10 digits, 01 to 05 by region
text: French telephone numbers are 10 digits long, with the first two pairs of digits being two separate area codes, following two patterns:
- 01 is in Île-de-France and 02-05 goes **clockwise **from the northwest.
- 2X is in the far north, with the numbers generally increasing **anticlockwise**. 9X is an exception, being found both in the far northwest and far southeast.
Secondary area codes in Île-de-France can be seen on [this map](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/0d/Indicatif_telephonique_IDF.jpg/1280px-Indicatif_telephonique_IDF.jpg).
NOTE: Phone numbers beginning with 06-09 are not regional.
clues.summary: Ten digits starting with a regional code: 01 is the Paris area, 02 to 05 go clockwise from the northwest. Numbers starting 06 to 09 are not regional.

clues.title: Postal codes: first two digits are the department
text: Each department has an assigned number to it, arranged mostly [alphabetically](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Departments_of_France#Current_departments). This is most useful in postal codes, consisting of 5 digits, the first two representing the department they’re in.
NOTE: the same regional codes are used inside the right blue strip on [licence plates](https://maps.app.goo.gl/hdSg7fcVKbUGPcjP8).
clues.summary: Postal codes have 5 digits, the first two being the department number, mostly alphabetical. The same numbers appear in the blue strip on plates.

clues.title: Logos: each department has its own
text: Most departments have their own unique logo (formally called official flag), often containing stylized initials or the entire name. Notable infrastructure with department logos include [bus stops](https://maps.app.goo.gl/1CqFWtzhUqLV2k8n7), [kilometre markers](https://maps.app.goo.gl/JGY1Xwa8SvPyyV5A9), [trail banners](https://maps.app.goo.gl/kP4kjMrH3rK5gLSZ7), [directional signs](https://maps.app.goo.gl/QM5gqNqrRtf4gWRR6) and [signbacks](https://maps.app.goo.gl/ZHA8UMQL6eFzSNyP6). Learning what each logo looks like is not recommended for beginners, but it can be helpful to know what they stand for when scanning.

You can find the full list of logos [here](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flags_of_the_regions_of_France#French_Departments), or see them projected onto a map [here](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/0/06/Flag_Map_of_Departments_of_France_Version_2_%28Logo_Flags%29.png).
clues.summary: Most departments have their own logo, often with initials or the full name, on bus stops, km markers, trail banners, direction signs and signbacks. Useful to know what they stand for, but not for beginners.

clues.title: Flag: red and yellow with a cross, stripes
text: A red and yellow logo with an [Occitan cross](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Occitan_cross) and vertical stripes is the official flag of the Occitanie region.

The rest of the regions also have [logos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flags_of_the_regions_of_France#Regions), which appear less frequently. You can see them projected onto a map [here](https://i.imgur.com/DNYKa4L.png).
clues.summary: A red and yellow logo with a cross and vertical stripes is the flag of the southern region of Occitanie. Other regions have logos that appear less often.

clues.title: Flag: red and yellow horizontal stripes
text: A flag made up of red and yellow stripes, based on [the Senyera](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Senyera), is the official flag and department logo of **Pyrénées-Orientales**. You will often find the pattern used in coats of arms on street signs.
NOTE: The flag of [Provence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Provence) looks similar, but with [vertical](https://maps.app.goo.gl/CWTzNJaQNoRJwEDeA) stripes instead.
clues.summary: A flag of red and yellow horizontal stripes is the flag and department logo of the far-south Pyrenees department, often shown in coats of arms on street signs. Provence's flag is similar but vertical.

clues.title: Road: reddish-purple tinted asphalt
text: Roads with a significant** red**, **purple** or **burgundy** tint are most commonly found in an area between Paris and Dijon, with Normandy being a notable exception. The historical region of [**Burgundy**](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burgundy), which gave the name to the shade of red, roughly corresponds to the highlighted area.
NOTE: Normal roads may deceptively look reddish under some lighting, so use this with caution.
clues.summary: Roads with a clear red, purple or burgundy tint are mostly between Paris and Dijon, except Normandy. Normal roads can look reddish in some light, so be careful.

clues.title: Sign: dark green signposts and backs
text: **Dark green** road signposts and backs are most commonly found in Brittany and around Paris, but also various southern regions in the country.
NOTE: Beware that this, and the following coloured infrastructure can rarely be found in other parts of the country.
clues.summary: Dark green signposts and backs are most common in Brittany and around Paris, plus several southern regions. They can appear elsewhere.

clues.title: Sign: green sticker on dark green back
text: Signbacks in Eure-et-Loir may include a **green sticker**, the department’s logo. They’re usually placed on a dark green back, without a matching post.
clues.summary: In one department near Paris, signbacks may carry the green department logo, usually on a dark green back with a mismatched post.

clues.title: Route marker: D-road with decimal number
text: Still in Eure-et-Loir, this is also where D-roads with a **superscript number** are most common. On the map, these are expressed as decimals, e.g. D134.10 and D121.9.
NOTE: They are rarely found in other [departments](https://maps.app.goo.gl/FLC24eo6tV36Jn1D8).
clues.summary: In that same department D-roads with a superscript number are most common. On the map they show as decimals, like D134.10. Rare elsewhere.

clues.title: Sign: greyish green back on darker green post
text: A **greyish green** signback supported by a **darker green** post, is found in three areas: Brittany (Côtes-d'Armor and eastern half of Ille-et-Vilaine), Pyrénées-Atlantiques and rarely near the Alps.
clues.summary: A greyish green signback on a darker green post is found in three areas: Brittany (north coast and east), the southwest corner, and rarely near the Alps.

clues.title: Sign: dark green post, light green back
text: In the Pas-de-Calais department, you may find road signs with the following colour arrangement: a **dark green post** paired with a signback of a **lighter shade of green**, ranging from [matcha green](https://maps.app.goo.gl/cH9cbEYkyVwUMkEXA) to [greenish turquoise](https://maps.app.goo.gl/HVwoK8mut3XwKQ8g8). The [department’s logo](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/fr/6/64/Logo_62_pas_de_calais.jpg), a green and blue triangle, is occasionally present [on the signback](https://maps.app.goo.gl/RV2AH3h7Lq75MKu47).
NOTE: Under certain lighting, they can appear similar to the greyish road signs mentioned in the previous tip.
clues.summary: In the northern department of Pas-de-Calais, a dark green post with a lighter green back (matcha to turquoise), sometimes with a green and blue triangle logo. In some light it looks like the greyish signs.

clues.title: Sign: brown post and brown back
text: Road signs where both the** post** and **back** are painted **brown** are most commonly found in Seine-et-Marne, and rarely in Ille-et-Vilaine. It is more reliable when the post is **square**, however round signposts are equally common.
clues.summary: Signs where both post and back are brown are most common east of Paris (Seine-et-Marne), rarely in Brittany. More reliable with square posts, but round ones are as common.

clues.title: Sign: burgundy red parts on direction signs
text: Directional signs in Haute-Garonne often use **burgundy red attachments** and ornaments. This is sometimes paired with [yellow signposts](https://maps.app.goo.gl/zXUbPBqqsHJZaBvu7).
clues.summary: Direction signs in one southwestern department often have burgundy red fittings and ornaments, sometimes with yellow signposts.

clues.title: Sign: town entry and exit in one thick block
text: Most town entry signs in Marne follow a unique format: Instead of having [separate](https://maps.app.goo.gl/MK8LGR6zFBcdyG2M7) entry and exit signs, they are combined into a **single, noticeably thicker block**.
clues.summary: Town entry signs in one northeastern department combine entry and exit into one noticeably thicker block.

clues.title: Street sign: city name on street signs
text: Street signs in the metropolitan area of Paris often say the** name of the city**, which is generally atypical for street signs in France. The signs will often be made in a **modern design**, and many city names will be** river based**, notably named after Seine and Marne.
NOTE: This can be seen sporadically throughout the country, so consider other clues.
clues.summary: Street signs around Paris often show the city name, which is unusual elsewhere. They are often modern, and many names relate to the Seine or Marne. It also appears sporadically elsewhere.

clues.title: Walls: cuboid stone and mortar barriers
text: Cuboid barriers made of** stones** and mortar are commonly found on Corsica. While by no means unique to Corsica, it is good to consider the island when you see them in rounds with a plausible Mediterranean landscape.
NOTE: Stone barriers with a [rounded top](https://maps.app.goo.gl/VJ9vC1KXSVHkmqHbA) are not found on Corsica.
clues.summary: Cuboid stone-and-mortar barriers are common on Corsica. Not unique, but think of the island when you see them in Mediterranean land. Rounded-top stone barriers are not found there.

clues.title: Landscape: high southeast, flat north
text: This is a topographic map of France. Notably, the tallest mountains are found in the southeast and on the Spanish border. The north and the west coast is generally quite flat or rolling, while the southern half is often hillier.
clues.summary: The tallest mountains are in the southeast and along the Spanish border. The north and west coast are flat or rolling, and the south is hillier.

clues.title: Plants: tall hedges blocking the view
text: Rural roads surrounded by hedges blocking the view, reminiscent of the British Isles, are primarily found in the northwest, particularly in Normandy.
NOTE: Hedges by themselves are not sufficient for recognizing this area and are common all over France.
clues.summary: Rural roads with hedges blocking the view, like the British Isles, are mainly in the northwest, especially Normandy. Hedges alone are common everywhere.

clues.title: Plants: stone pines along the south coast
text: [**Stone pines**](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stone_pine) are commonly found along the southern coast, often planted alongside urban roads. You may however find them as north as Nantes.
clues.summary: Stone pines grow along the south coast, often planted along city roads. They can be found as far north as Nantes.

clues.title: Plants: pure maritime pine forests, flat
text: Forests made up entirely of Maritime pines ([pinus pinaster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pinus_pinaster)) are found in the southwest of the country (Gironde and Landes departments). The whole area will be fairly flat, which is not typical of other areas with such pines.
clues.summary: Forests made entirely of maritime pines are in the southwest (Gironde and Landes), on very flat land, unlike other pine areas.

clues.title: Plants: vineyards
text: France is the second largest wine producer in the world, with many famed wine regions. The most common include the area [around Bordeaux](https://maps.app.goo.gl/m8uNroZ9jJLd3QAK9), [southern coast](https://maps.app.goo.gl/HTsrjHu2c5PRFyf66) and [Champagne](https://maps.app.goo.gl/qtGYHb1vJigF6dhh8), East of Paris. Other regions include, but are not limited to, [Loire Valley](https://maps.app.goo.gl/DfoQ5ieYBdvu3Gwj6), [Alsace](https://maps.app.goo.gl/VZ83XTNAHMGyYnpo7) and [Corsica](https://maps.app.goo.gl/1LfT57wVaQ6dhW4f7).
NOTE: This map is highly simplified, see [this map](https://vineyards.com/photos/maps/France%20Wine%20Map.png) for more detailed and extensive description.
clues.summary: France is the second biggest wine producer. Main areas: around Bordeaux, the south coast and Champagne east of Paris. Others: Loire Valley, Alsace and Corsica.

clues.title: Plants: sunflowers
text: **Sunflowers** are mostly found in the southwest of the country, particularly around Toulouse.
clues.summary: Sunflowers are mostly in the southwest, especially around Toulouse.

clues.title: Landmark: wind turbines in the north
text: Wind turbines are considerably more common in the north of the country.
clues.summary: Wind turbines are far more common in the north.

clues.title: Roofs: black shingles in the northwest
text: **Black shingle roofs** are primarily found in the northwest, the rough cutoff being the Loire river. Other areas include near the Belgian border, the south-centre, and the Pyrenees, making black roofs a good clue for Alps-Pyrenees toss-ups.
clues.summary: Black shingle roofs are mainly in the northwest, cut off roughly at the Loire. Also near the Belgian border, south-centre and Pyrenees, so black roofs help in Alps vs Pyrenees choices.

clues.title: Houses: Brittany style, black roofs, edge chimneys
text: **Brittany** has one of the most recognizable and consistent architectures in the country. Common elements include, in addition to black roofs, [edge chimneys](https://maps.app.goo.gl/aAhwWVjHEPsQPH9T6), [black slate walls](https://maps.app.goo.gl/HepcAWsvqucqhSpb6) and [stones surrounding doors and windows](https://maps.app.goo.gl/aMX5LbsbQsab7LmT9). The walls will be either very light coloured or made of stone.
clues.summary: A very consistent style: black roofs, chimneys on the gable edge, black slate walls and stone around doors and windows. Walls are very light or stone.

clues.title: Roofs: overlapping rounded tiles in the south
text: Roofs in the south of the country will often be made up of rounded tiles overlapping one another, often varying in colour.
clues.summary: Roofs in the south are often made of overlapping rounded tiles, often in varied colours.

clues.title: Houses: dark red brick rows near Belgium
text: Rows of dark red brick houses, most similar to Flemish architecture in Belgium, are unsurprisingly found near the Belgian border. The individual bricks may be outlined by white mortar.
clues.summary: Rows of dark red brick houses, like Flemish ones in Belgium, are near the Belgian border. Bricks may be outlined with white mortar.

differs.how: similar bricks, use plates and language

clues.title: Houses: bright orange brick, shutters
text: In and around Toulouse, mainly in old towns, you will commonly find **bright orange brick buildings**. They differ from brick houses near Belgium by the bricks being brighter, as well as somewhat Mediterranean looking architectural features, such as [wooden shutters](https://maps.app.goo.gl/1Bp6ctTT9uJVuXX67), being common.
clues.summary: In old towns around Toulouse you often see bright orange brick buildings, brighter than the northern ones, with Mediterranean touches like wooden shutters.

clues.title: Houses: cream and orange stone, red brick details
text: Walls made of uneven **cream coloured **to **orange stones**, glued with mortar and often incorporating **red brick details** can be found in the towns surrounding Paris. Note that the city of Paris itself generally does not have this architecture.
clues.summary: Uneven cream-to-orange stone walls with mortar and red brick details are in the towns around Paris, but usually not in Paris itself.

clues.title: Houses: palms, light multi-storey buildings, balconies
text: The [French Riviera](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_Riviera) will mirror many characteristics of Monaco. Rich areas with planted **palms** and light coloured multi story buildings with **wide balconies** are good indications you’re in this area, with the rest of the southern coast and Corsican Bastia sharing similar vibes.
NOTE: Just like Monaco, several cities host [boat trekkers](https://maps.app.goo.gl/KMhr7HRhd1ch44jR6) in their harbour.
clues.summary: The Riviera looks like Monaco: wealthy areas with planted palms and light multi-storey buildings with wide balconies. Other southern coast towns feel similar. Several harbours have boat trekkers.

differs.how: looks the same, use plates and signs

clues.title: Houses: white walls, coloured timber frames
text: White houses with, often colourful, timber framing are a staple of Basque architecture that extends beyond the Basque speaking area. The timber frame colour (in this case red) will be consistent with other wooden elements, like window shutters and gates.
NOTE: They’re also common in parts of Northern Spain, where the timber frames are usually unpainted.
clues.summary: White houses with often colourful timber framing, matching shutters and gates, are typical of the Basque area and beyond. Northern Spain has them too, but with unpainted timber.

differs.how: timber frames are usually unpainted

clues.title: Houses: light base, lots of wood
text: Alpine architecture, unmistakable for its light coloured base and extensive **wooden** elements, is unsurprisingly found in the Alps.
NOTE: Similar houses can be found in the [touristic parts of Pyrenees](https://maps.app.goo.gl/gBufc9meA3Qc2Z7eA).
clues.summary: Alpine houses have a light base and lots of wood. Similar houses exist in tourist parts of the Pyrenees.

clues.title: Houses: timber frames, half-hip, fish-scale tiles
text: Many elements of** Germanic architecture** are concentrated in Alsace, such as **timber framing** and [half-hip roof](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hip_roof#Half-hip_roof). Furthermore, roofs with [fish scale tiles](https://maps.app.goo.gl/awYyavUYj1kHHdVX7) are more common in this region.
Beware that these elements are sometimes incorporated into [architecture](https://maps.app.goo.gl/c72CRemeuSDxuZfE8) in other parts of France, and are most reliable in conjunction with one another.
clues.summary: German-style elements in the east: timber framing, half-hip roofs and fish-scale tiles. They appear elsewhere sometimes, so look for several together.

clues.title: Language: six minority languages
text: France is home to many minority languages, 6 of which will be covered in this guide:
- **Alsatian**, a dialect of Alemannic German.
- **Basque**, the only European [language isolate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Language_isolate).
- **Breton**, a Celtic language.
- **Catalan, Corsican **and **Occitan**, Romance languages which are related to French.
However, French, legally the only official language, is dominant in all regions of the country, so don’t exclude highlighted regions when you’re placed in an all French round.
clues.summary: Six minority languages: Alsatian, Basque, Breton, Catalan, Corsican and Occitan. French dominates everywhere, so don't rule out regions in all-French rounds.

clues.title: Language: Celtic, d k w and ñ
text: [**Breton**](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_language) is a Celtic language, visually most similar to Welsh. Common letters include **d**, **k**, **w **and the letter** ñ**, which is not found in French. It is commonly found on the Breton peninsula, with bilingual street signs as east as [Rennes](https://maps.app.goo.gl/SXA9tpudgXLcbpvJ7) and rarely [Nantes](https://maps.app.goo.gl/v9hAN6FqvpLekm5n6). The Breton word for street is straed**.**
clues.summary: Breton is Celtic and looks like Welsh, with letters d, k, w and ñ. It appears on bilingual signs across Brittany, as far east as Rennes, rarely Nantes. Its word for street is straed.

differs.how: looks like Welsh, but uses ñ

clues.title: Towns: names starting with Plou-
text: Towns with the **Plou-** prefix are concentrated in Northwestern Brittany.
clues.summary: Towns whose names start with Plou- are in the northwest of Brittany.

clues.title: Language: German-like signs, gasse or strasse
text: [**Alsatian**](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alsatian_dialect), a dialect of German, is occasionally found in [Alsace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alsace), a region that changed countries 4 times in modern history. Most bilingual street signs use some variation of gasse or strasse.
NOTE: Streets [containing German names](https://maps.app.goo.gl/jEGWQJfdTYS2sMK18) are also concentrated in this region, though not as consistently.
clues.summary: Alsatian, a German dialect, shows on bilingual signs in the east using gasse or strasse. Streets with German names are also concentrated there.

clues.title: Language: Occitan, carrer-like street word
text: [**Occitan**](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Occitan_language) is a Romance language closely related to Catalan that’s sparsely concentrated in the South of France, most often found on street signs in big cities, and very rarely on [town entry signs](https://maps.app.goo.gl/J5Bj9ZSR2MfHAegg9). It can be divided into dialects, each using a slightly different word for street, all similar to Catalan “carrer”. For example, in Toulouse, you’ll find the Languedocian carrièra and in Avignon carriero, in the Provençal** **dialect.
Click [here](https://i.imgur.com/B8gX96p.png) for a more extensive infographic.
NOTE: The street sign designs pictured are also unique to the two cities respectively.
clues.summary: Occitan is close to Catalan, spread thinly in the south, mostly on city street signs. Street words like 'carrièra' (southwest) and 'carriero' (southeast coast) resemble Catalan 'carrer'.

clues.title: Language: Basque, K X Z, thin font
text: Bilingual signs in [**Basque**](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Basque_language), a language isolate, are concentrated In the western half of the Pyrénées-Atlantiques department, bordering the Basque speaking regions in Spain. Common letters include K, X and Z. On directional signs, it’s written with a **thinner font**, which is unique within all minority languages in France.
The word for street is karrika, in contrast to “kalea” in the Spanish Basque country.
clues.summary: Basque signs are in the western half of the Pyrenees department next to Spanish Basque country. Common letters are K, X and Z, and direction signs use a thinner font. Street is karrika, not Spain's kalea.

differs.how: Spanish Basque country uses 'kalea' for street

clues.title: Language: Italian-like words ending in u
text: On the island of Corsica, you may find bilingual signs in [**Corsican**](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corsican_language), a Romance language that utilises many features found in Italian, like words almost always ending in vowels. In particular, the endings** u/iu/ju**, changed from o/io, are common in Corsican. Moreover, placenames will usually have an Italian origin.
clues.summary: On Corsica you find signs in Corsican, close to Italian, with words ending in vowels and endings -u, -iu, -ju. Place names often have Italian origins.

clues.title: Language: Catalan, word 'carrer'
text: The far southern department **Pyrénées-Orientales**, also known as Catalunya Nord (Northern Catalonia), uses [**Catalan**](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catalan_language) on their various signage.
It is closely related to both Spanish and French, with Ç being considerably more common than in French. The word for street is carrer.
clues.summary: The far southern department uses Catalan, close to Spanish and French, with more Ç than French. Street is 'carrer'.

clues.title: Town names: common endings by region
text: Knowing basic toponymy in France is crucial for regionguessing, particularly suffixes. This map shows one of the most common and useful endings, with rare exceptions. Other, extraordinarily rare suffixes can be found [here](/images/france/2_minortoponyms.png?).
_You can click on the image to enlarge it._
clues.summary: Place name endings are crucial for guessing the region. The map shows the most common ones, with a few exceptions.

clues.title: Town names: -sur-river, -sur-mer, -plage
text: Many French cities contain the name of the **river** they lay on, usually in the format **-sur-[river]**. On signage, sur are often [shortened to ˢ/](https://maps.app.goo.gl/KZQRgQ7Pszn6X79R6), in this case Chalonnes-sur-Loire (Chalonnes upon Loire). The picture shows five of the longest and therefore most common origins of river based names, but cities can bear the name of any river, regardless of length.

Similarly, city names containing [-sur-mer](https://maps.app.goo.gl/nKqfxeaX1hhikGeF8) (=on sea) or [-plage](https://maps.app.goo.gl/6mbr4tT9J4CRaEAb8) (=beach)** **are found exclusively on the coast.
clues.summary: Many cities carry their river name, like Chalonnes-sur-Loire (sur is often shortened). Names with -sur-mer or -plage are only on the coast.

clues.title: Location: island east of Madagascar
text: Réunion is an overseas department and region of France, east of Madagascar. As such, it is counted as France for country streaks purposes.
Plonk It has a more in-depth guide to Réunion [here](https://www.plonkit.net/reunion).
clues.summary: An overseas department east of Madagascar. It counts as France for country streaks.

differs.how: Madagascar is a separate country

clues.title: Location: islands south of Newfoundland
text: Saint-Pierre and Miquelon is a self-governing territorial overseas collectivity of France, south of Newfoundland in Canada. As such, for country streaks purposes, it is counted as France.
Plonk It has a more in-depth guide to Saint-Pierre and Miquelon [here](https://www.plonkit.net/saint-pierre-and-miquelon).
clues.summary: A self-governing territory of France south of Newfoundland in Canada. It counts as France for streaks.

differs.how: Canada is a separate country

clues.title: Location: eastern Caribbean island
text: Martinique is an overseas department and region and a single territorial collectivity of France, in the eastern Caribbean. For country streaks purposes, it is counted as France.
Plonk It has a more in-depth guide to Martinique [here](https://www.plonkit.net/martinique).
clues.summary: An overseas department in the eastern Caribbean. It counts as France for streaks.

clues.title: Roofs: steep black mansard with dormer windows
text: [Mansard roofs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mansard_roof), also known as French windows, are a very common feature of Parisian architecture. They’re made up of steep black shingle roofs with inserted dormer windows. While not unique to Paris, it is a good clue in abundance and on wide boulevards.
clues.summary: Steep black shingle mansard roofs with dormer windows are very common in the capital. Not unique, but a good clue in large numbers and on wide boulevards.

clues.title: Houses: Breton houses with colourful fronts
text: On the Breton island** Belle-Île-en-Mer** you can find houses typical for Brittany combined with colourful façades and outlines, superficially similar to houses in Portugal.
NOTE: The entire island was only covered with an often oversaturated Generation 2 camera.
clues.summary: On one Breton island, local-style houses have colourful façades and outlines, a bit like Portugal. The island has only oversaturated Gen 2 coverage.

differs.how: similar colourful houses, but Gen 2 camera here

clues.title: Plants: lavender fields
text: **Lavender fields** can be found in the southeast, appearing as [small grey bushes](https://maps.app.goo.gl/Mm9eUmvDpzN6izC57) when not fully grown.
clues.summary: Lavender fields grow in the southeast and look like small grey bushes when young.

clues.title: Landscape: salt farms along the Atlantic coast
text: **Salt farms**, which appear as flooded trenches with grass medians, are found along the Atlantic coast, most notably around Guérande, Noirmoutier, Île de Ré and Île d'Oléron.
clues.summary: Salt farms look like flooded trenches with grass strips between them. Found along the Atlantic coast, notably Guérande, Noirmoutier, Île de Ré and Île d'Oléron.

clues.title: Street sign: 'Arr' district on the big three
text: **Paris**, **Lyon** and **Marseille** are the three largest cities in France and the only ones divided into **municipal arrondissements **(Arrᵗ or Arrt.** **for short). The arrondissements appear on google maps, so finding these street signs can help a lot with pinpointing.
The street signs of these three cities will be further described in the following tips.
clues.summary: Paris, Lyon and Marseille are the only cities split into arrondissements (shown as Arrᵗ or Arrt.). The district shows on the map, which helps pinpoint.

clues.title: Street sign: green and Prussian blue with arch
text: Paris uses an iconic** green & Prussian blue **design with a top arch that has also been replicated in [Bucharest](https://maps.app.goo.gl/E3LqAPwX8jt9YmgK8), which is sometimes referred to as Paris of the east.
NOTE: The simple rectangular form of the sign can be found in the [towns nearby](https://maps.app.goo.gl/Noo6GyM9T63fta8C8) and rarely in [other cities](https://maps.app.goo.gl/SN1rqVG9eMNqQZxQ8).
clues.summary: Paris uses an iconic green and Prussian blue sign with an arched top, copied in Bucharest. The plain rectangle appears in nearby towns and rarely elsewhere.

differs.how: Bucharest copies the Paris sign; check language

clues.title: Street sign: four corner bolts, notched white border
text: Lyon’s street signs feature four corner bolts and an **uninterrupted inner white border** that cuts a **notch** for the arrondissement and each bolt.
NOTE: Outside Lyon proper, the street sign will display the [name of the suburb](https://maps.app.goo.gl/gP3ngUUpUKf4Rqmz6) instead.
clues.summary: Lyon's signs have four corner bolts and an unbroken inner white border with notches for the district and each bolt. Outside Lyon proper the suburb name is shown.

clues.title: Street sign: city emblem, Greek-style cross
text: **Marseille**’s street signs will usually feature the city’s **emblem**, a variation of the [Greek cross](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christian_cross_variants#Greek_cross). The white border will usually be **interrupted** at the top, even when the cross is [absent](https://maps.app.goo.gl/Kb4vaENAKeNfGt2XA).
clues.summary: Marseille's street signs usually carry the city emblem, a variation of the Greek cross, and the white border is broken at the top even if the cross is missing.

clues.title: Street sign: small 'Arr' plate in a non-split city
text: Small tables with “**Arrᵗ**” written on a small separate sign, are found in **Bordeaux**, despite being a city not divided into arrondissements.
clues.summary: Small tables saying 'Arrᵗ' on a separate sign are found in Bordeaux, even though it has no arrondissements.

clues.title: Street sign: blue M on white, top left
text: **Montpellier** street signs will typically contain a blue **‘M’** on a white background in the top left corner.
clues.summary: Street signs with a blue 'M' on a white background in the top left corner mean Montpellier.

clues.title: Street sign: red slanted fleur-de-lis
text: Street signs with a red slanted [fleur-de-lis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fleur-de-lis) are unique to **Lille**.
clues.summary: Street signs with a red slanted fleur-de-lis are unique to Lille.

clues.title: Sign: wine-red square signposts
text: In the outskirts of **Bordeaux**, you may find square traffic signposts with the [Bordeaux](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wine_red#Claret) shade of **red**, named after the wine grown in the region.
NOTE: Red posts by themselves are not unique to Bordeaux, so apply this meta with caution.
clues.summary: On the edge of Bordeaux, square traffic signposts are in wine red. Red posts alone are not unique, so use with caution.

clues.title: Sign: azure blue signposts
text: On the French Riviera (Côte d'Azur in French, literally translated as **Blue Coast**), you can find regular traffic signposts painted azure blue. Uniquely, [Cagnes-sur-mer](https://maps.app.goo.gl/sP2LGFRxb79XRWro6), west of Nice, will feature lighter, powder blue infrastructure.
NOTE: Blue infrastructure can be found to a lesser extent all across France, particularly [Brittany](https://maps.app.goo.gl/6GwpcWAD5gS5LCE7A), so consider the landscape as well.
clues.summary: On the Riviera, regular traffic signposts are painted azure blue, and one town west of Nice has lighter powder blue ones. Blue infrastructure appears elsewhere, especially Brittany, so check the landscape.

clues.title: Guardrail: thin B-type on northern highways
text: **Thin B type** guardrail, typical for Czechia and Slovakia, is sometimes found on **highways** in the northern half of the country, often coming from Le Mans, Tours, Paris, Reims and Metz.

NOTE: On the highlighted sections, thin B can be the minority guardrail, and short sections of any highway will have no guardrails at all. It is also more common on smaller roads in the North, but less consistent as a clue.
clues.summary: Thin B-type guardrail, standard in Czechia and Slovakia, is sometimes found on northern highways from Le Mans, Tours, Paris, Reims and Metz. Often a minority there, and more common but less reliable on small northern roads.

differs.how: Czech Republic uses thin B-type as standard
Slovakia uses thin B-type as standard

clues.title: Pole: spiked top on wooden poles
text: It is sometimes hard to distinguish France, Ireland, and the UK. An easy trick is to focus on the tops of the wooden poles: France has a spiked top.

clues.title: Plate: yellow front plates near Luxembourg
text: France can sometimes have **yellow back license plates**, especially in old coverage. Should you see several yellow plates **on the front**, you're probably near Luxembourg.

clues.title: Landscape: very flat industrial fields, no hedges
text: La Beauce is one of the flattest regions of France, located South of Paris.

Apart from the flatness of the area, the important thing to notice about the fields in the Beauce region is that they are industrialized. You will not see hedges around the fields like you could see in the West of France. So, if you see very flat and industrialized fields with potatoes or cereals, you can be in this area. Still, the Paris hedge remains good because there are many fields North and East of Paris (but you will never get a 5K by guessing Paris out of fields).

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.summary: The Beauce region south of Paris is one of the flattest, with industrial-size fields of potatoes or cereals and no hedges, unlike the west.

clues.title: Animals: cows, horses and sheep
text: It is not so rare to see cows, horses, or sheep in France in Geoguessr. If that ever happens, you should consider the West of the country (Brittany, Normandy), as well as the mountainous regions (Pyrenees and Alps). This is where you have the most chances to find animals in France in Google Street View.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.summary: Livestock is most often seen in the west (Brittany, Normandy) and in the mountains (Pyrenees, Alps).
